NDT training in Vermont: how it works for Vermont employers and technicians

Short answer: Atlantis NDT delivers ASNT SNT-TC-1A-based Level I, II and III training in UT, PAUT, TOFD, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET for Vermont employers and technicians. We have no classroom in Vermont. Theory runs live online or in scheduled cohorts, and practical training runs onsite at your facility under ASNT Level III oversight. That suits a state where most NDT employers are small, spread out and far from any training school.

Vermont's NDT market is not a refinery corridor, and pretending otherwise helps no one. It is a small-state market of specialists. There is aerospace component manufacturing, including engine airfoils and aircraft systems. There is a semiconductor fab at Essex Junction. There is a nuclear plant at Vernon in the late stages of decommissioning. There are precision machine shops supplying defence and aerospace primes, an electric-aircraft developer near Burlington, hydroelectric dams, a state bridge inventory rebuilt and strengthened after major floods, and ski areas whose lifts need regular component inspection. Most of these employers need a handful of qualified people rather than dozens, and that shapes how training should be delivered.

For a Vermont technician, it is the travel that hurts. Sending one person to a week-long course in another state costs lodging and lost production, and the courses rarely match the parts they actually inspect. For a Vermont employer, the harder problem is usually the certification system itself. SNT-TC-1A needs a written practice and a Level III to administer examinations, and a company with three inspectors rarely employs a Level III. This page explains how both problems are solved.

To get started, request a Vermont training quote. Cohort and onsite quotes come back within one business day.

ASNT Level I, II and III courses available in Vermont

Courses follow SNT-TC-1A topical outlines and document classroom hours for your written practice. The table maps methods to typical Vermont applications. It shows common uses, not any employer's stated requirements.

MethodLevelsWhat Vermont employers use it forPrerequisite
UT (ultrasonic testing)I, II, III prepBridge and structural weld examination, thickness surveys on penstocks and dam components, forged and machined part inspectionNone for Level I; Level II requires Level I plus documented experience
PAUT (phased array)II, III prepStructural and bridge weld examination, complex machined and forged geometries, weld inspection on fabricated componentsUsually UT Level II per the written practice
TOFD (time-of-flight diffraction)II, III prepThick-section welds on heavy fabrications and pressure equipmentUsually UT Level II
RT (radiographic testing)I, II, III prepCastings and welded components for aerospace and industrial customers, weld radiography on piping and pressure workNone for Level I; Vermont radiation-control requirements apply separately to source users
MT (magnetic particle)I, II, III prepFerromagnetic machined parts, lift components such as shafts and grips, structural steel and bridge weldsNone for Level I
PT (liquid penetrant)I, II, III prepAerospace airfoils and non-magnetic components, precision-machined parts, stainless weldsNone for Level I
VT (visual testing)I, II, III prepBridge and dam condition inspection, weld visual, component acceptance in manufacturingNone for Level I
ET (eddy current)I, II, III prepSurface-crack inspection on aerospace parts and fastener holes, conductivity and material sorting in machine shopsNone for Level I

PT, ET and MT are the core methods for Vermont's aerospace and precision-manufacturing employers. Turbine airfoils, aircraft system components and machined parts are inspected for surface-breaking discontinuities throughout production. Many aerospace employers qualify inspectors under NAS 410 or customer-specific schemes, and some Vermont employers ask for that. Atlantis training is SNT-TC-1A-based, so check with your Level III whether the classroom hours can be credited under the scheme you work to.

UT in Vermont covers everything from forged-part inspection in manufacturing to weld examination on bridges and thickness surveys on hydro penstocks. Level I covers theory, straight-beam work and calibration. Level II adds angle-beam weld examination, evaluation to acceptance criteria and reporting.

PAUT and TOFD are Level II-and-above courses for UT-qualified technicians. In Vermont they are most relevant to structural and bridge fabrication, heavy welded components and firms bidding on work that specifies encoded ultrasonic examination.

RT is used on castings and welds for manufacturing customers and on pressure and piping work. The NDT course covers technique and interpretation. Radiation-safety requirements for source users are regulated by the state and are covered separately below.

VT underpins every other method and is the main method in bridge and dam condition work. Candidates heading for Level III can use our ASNT Level III exam preparation. See all courses on the NDT training programmes page.

SNT-TC-1A certification path in Vermont, step by step

Under SNT-TC-1A, the employer grants certification. For a Vermont machine shop with two inspectors or a bridge contractor with a small QC team, the steps are the same as for a large company. The difference is who does the Level III work.

  1. Have a written practice. It states which methods and levels you certify, training and experience minimums, exam rules, the responsible Level III and the recertification cycle. Aerospace and defence customers commonly ask to see it during supplier audits.
  2. Complete formal classroom training. Atlantis delivers this online, in cohorts or onsite. The required hours come from your written practice, normally based on SNT-TC-1A's recommendations. See the training requirements matrix.
  3. Build documented experience. Hours performing the method under supervision, logged and verified. In a small shop, a good log matters even more because there are fewer people to vouch for the work.
  4. Pass general, specific and practical examinations. General covers theory. Specific covers your procedures, equipment and the codes or customer specifications you work to. Practical is performed on real specimens and graded by or under a Level III, who can be an outside Level III.
  5. Pass the vision examination. Near-vision acuity and colour contrast, repeated as the written practice requires.
  6. Receive employer certification. Signed by your company's certifying authority on the Level III's recommendation.
  7. Recertify on time. Within the interval in your written practice.

The SNT-TC-1A training and certification guide explains each step, including how small employers use an outside Level III.

Online, live-virtual or onsite NDT training for Vermont crews

Atlantis has no physical training centre in Vermont, and for a state with Vermont's geography, a single fixed centre would not help most employers anyway. We deliver three ways.

  • Live online theory. Real-time, instructor-led classes for the classroom portion, taken from anywhere with a reliable connection. For a technician in Rutland, St. Albans or Brattleboro, that removes most of the travel burden. See NDT training online.
  • Classroom cohorts. When enough candidates share a method and level, at an arranged venue.
  • Onsite at your facility. The instructor comes to your shop, plant or yard and runs practical sessions on your equipment and components. For aerospace and precision manufacturers, that means training on the actual part geometries and surface finishes your inspectors see.

Vermont scheduling has its own rhythm. Bridge and construction inspection work peaks in the construction season from spring to autumn. Ski-area maintenance falls mostly in the off-season before lifts open. Manufacturers schedule around production and customer deliveries. We usually run online theory in winter or during slower production periods and book onsite practical sessions when your people can be released. Small groups are not a problem. Onsite delivery is often the most sensible option even for two or three technicians, because it avoids sending people out of state.

Ask about onsite training for your Vermont team. Employers training across several sites can see our corporate NDT training programmes.

Where NDT technicians work in Vermont

Aerospace and precision manufacturing. Vermont has a long aerospace manufacturing history. GE Aerospace has engine-component manufacturing in Rutland, Collins Aerospace operates in Vergennes, and a network of precision machine shops supplies aerospace and defence primes. Surface NDT (PT, MT, ET) is used throughout production, with UT and RT for forgings, castings and welded assemblies. Many of these employers work to NAS 410 or customer-specific qualification requirements, and some also hold Nadcap NDT accreditation. Those schemes sit alongside, or instead of, SNT-TC-1A depending on the customer.

Electric aviation. BETA Technologies, based at Burlington International Airport in South Burlington, is developing and building electric aircraft. That brings aerospace-style manufacturing and inspection work to the Burlington area.

Semiconductors. The GlobalFoundries fab in Essex Junction is one of Vermont's largest private employers. Fab facilities have piping, pressure systems and structural work that uses conventional NDT through facilities teams and contractors, though most process-tool inspection falls outside classical NDT.

Nuclear decommissioning. The Vermont Yankee plant in Vernon shut down in 2014 and is being decommissioned by NorthStar. Spent fuel is stored in dry casks at an on-site storage installation that remains under NRC jurisdiction. Remaining inspection work is specialised and governed by NRC-regulated programmes.

Bridges, dams and infrastructure. The Vermont Agency of Transportation maintains a large bridge inventory that was heavily rebuilt after Tropical Storm Irene in 2011, and flooding in July 2023 caused further damage. Steel bridge fabrication and rehabilitation run on AWS D1.5 with VT, MT and UT. Structural steel work generally follows AWS D1.1. Vermont's hydroelectric dams and penstocks also need periodic inspection.

Ski lifts and tramways. Vermont's ski areas run aerial lifts regulated by the state's Passenger Tramway Safety Board, generally in line with the ANSI B77.1 standard. Lift maintenance programmes commonly include NDT of critical components such as shafts, pins and grips, mostly MT and UT. This is seasonal, specialised work, and a good fit for technicians who already hold MT or UT.

Military. The Vermont Air National Guard's fighter wing at Burlington maintains its aircraft through military NDI programmes. Airmen leaving that career field often convert their experience to civilian certification.

Radiography licensing in Vermont. Vermont became an NRC Agreement State in 2019. The Vermont Department of Health's Radiological Health Program now licenses most radioactive materials use in the state, including industrial radiography sources. Vermont Yankee stays under NRC jurisdiction. Out-of-state radiography companies working in Vermont need reciprocity. Radiation-safety training and radiographer certification are separate from SNT-TC-1A RT certification, and a radiographer needs both.

A note for cross-border work. Vermont borders Quebec, where aerospace and industrial employers work to Canada's national scheme, CAN/CGSB-48.9712 (based on ISO 9712), administered through Natural Resources Canada. Atlantis training is SNT-TC-1A-based and suits employers working to US codes and US customers. It is not CGSB-recognised, and we do not claim otherwise.

For pay by level and method, see our NDT salary guide.

Level III services and written practices for Vermont NDT companies

Vermont's typical NDT employer is a manufacturer or contractor with a small inspection team and no Level III on staff. Under SNT-TC-1A, that works if the company has a compliant written practice and an outside Level III who administers examinations and signs off on certification records. Where it fails is when the written practice was copied from another company, covers methods the shop does not perform, or has not been updated for the current SNT-TC-1A edition. Aerospace and defence supplier audits find these gaps quickly.

  • Written practice development. We draft or revise a written practice sized for your company, covering the methods you perform, the customer specifications you work to, and realistic training and experience requirements. See written practice development.
  • Outside Level III services. Examination administration, procedure and technique review, and certification-record maintenance, delivered remotely where possible and onsite where it has to be.
  • Supplier audit preparation. A review of training records, experience logs, exam files and vision tests before customer or third-party audits.

Book a Level III consultation for your Vermont company, and read our SNT-TC-1A guidance.

Practise before the practical exam

For candidates who have trained mostly online, the practical exam is the biggest hurdle. The Practical NDT 3D simulator lets trainees practise 12 methods in five environments: an NDT lab, a welding workshop, an aircraft hangar, an oil and gas site and a storage tank. Vermont aerospace candidates will find the hangar and lab environments most relevant, and structural and fabrication candidates the welding workshop.

It is for practice only. The simulator does not replace hands-on practical training or the practical exam on real specimens under a Level III. For written preparation, see our UT Level 2 practice questions and related method sets.

Your instructor

Courses are led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. Anoop authors course content to SNT-TC-1A topical outlines and oversees practical sessions and examinations as the responsible Level III. Vermont employers planning onsite programmes work with him directly on scope and scheduling.

Frequently asked questions about NDT training in Vermont

How do I get NDT certified in Vermont?

Choose a method relevant to Vermont employers, such as PT, MT or ET for manufacturing, or UT and VT for structural work. Complete formal Level I training, build documented experience and pass your employer's general, specific and practical exams and a vision test. Your employer then certifies you under its written practice.

Can I take NDT training online in Vermont?

Yes. The classroom portion runs as live online classes, which works well in a rural state. Practical training and exams must be hands-on, and we deliver those onsite at your employer's facility. See NDT training online.

How long does UT Level 2 training take?

It depends on the classroom and experience hours in your employer's written practice, usually based on SNT-TC-1A recommendations. Classroom hours are the shorter part. Experience takes longer, especially in a smaller shop. See the training requirements matrix.

Do I need a license for radiography in Vermont?

Companies using radioactive sources need a licence from the Vermont Department of Health, which has regulated radioactive materials since Vermont became an Agreement State in 2019. Individual radiographers must meet radiation-safety training and certification requirements. SNT-TC-1A RT certification is a separate NDT credential.

What does NDT training cost in Vermont?

We do not publish prices. Cost depends on method, level, number of candidates and whether training is online, in a cohort or onsite. Request a Vermont training quote and you will receive a quote within one business day.

Is ASNT certification recognised by Vermont employers?

SNT-TC-1A is widely used by US industrial, structural and many manufacturing employers. Some aerospace employers use NAS 410 or customer-specific schemes. SNT-TC-1A certification is employer-based, so a new employer recertifies you under its own written practice.

Is training worth it for a company with only two or three inspectors?

Yes. Onsite delivery to a small group avoids out-of-state travel, and pairing it with an outside Level III gives a small company a complete, auditable certification system.

Does Atlantis have a training centre in Vermont?

No. We deliver live online theory, cohorts at arranged venues and onsite training at your facility.

Can I use Atlantis training to work in Quebec?

Quebec and the rest of Canada use CAN/CGSB-48.9712. Atlantis training is SNT-TC-1A-based and is not CGSB-recognised. It suits US employers and Canadian employers working to US codes for US clients.

Do you train for ski-lift NDT?

Our MT and UT courses cover the methods commonly used on lift components. Specific procedures and acceptance criteria come from the lift manufacturer, applicable standards and the operator's maintenance programme, which can be built into onsite practical sessions.

Do you offer NAS 410, CWI or ISO 9712 courses?

No. Atlantis trains to ASNT SNT-TC-1A only. Those schemes are obtained separately.

How do I prepare for ASNT Level III?

Use our Level III exam preparation, covering the Basic exam and method exams.
